source_text: Quibus duobus dominis neget posse seruiri, quia alterum offendi sit necesse alterum defendi, ipse declarat, deum proponens et mamonam. proinde mamonam quem intellegi uelit, si interpretem non habes, ab ipso potes discere. admonens enim nos de saecularibus suffragia nobis prospicere amicitiarum secundum serui illius exemplum, qui ab actu summotus dominicos debitores diminutis cautionibus releuat in subsidium sibi: et ego, inquit, dico uobis, facite uobis amicos de mamona iniustitiae, de nummo scilicet, de ' quo et seruus ille. iniustitiae enim auctorem et dominatorem totius saeculi nummum scimus omnes. cui famulatam uidens Pharisaeorum cupiditatem ammentauit hanc sententiam: non potestis deo seruire et mamonae. inridebant denique Pharisaei pecuniae cupidi, quod intellexissent scilicet mamonam de nummo dictum, ne quia existimet in mamona creatorem intellegendum et Christum a creatoris illos seruitute reuocasse.. quid nunc? potius ex hoc disce unum a Christo deum ostensum. duos enim dominos nominauit, deum et mamonam, crea. torem et nummum: denique non potestis deo seruire, utique ei, cui uidebantur seruire, et mamonam, cui magis destinabantur. quodsi ipse alium se ageret, non duos dominos, sed tres demonstrasset — et creator enim dominus, quia deus, et utique magis dominus quam mamonas magisque homini obseruandus, qua magis dominus —; quale est enim, ut qui mamonam dominum dixerat et cum domino iunxerat uero, ipsum dominum taceret, id est deum creatorem? aut numquid tacendo eo concessit seruiendum ei esse, si solummodo sibi et mamonae negauit posse seruiri? ita cum unum deum ponit, nominaturus et creatorem, si alius esset ipse, creatorem nominauit quem [dominum] sine alio [deo non] posuit. et illud itaque relucebit, quomodo dictum sit: (si) in mamona iniusto fideles non extitistis, quod uerum est quis uobis credet? in nummo scilicet iniusto, non in creatore, quem et Marcion iustum facit, et: si in alieno fideles inuenti non estis, meum quis dabit uobis? alienum enim debet esse a semis dei quod iniustum est. creator autem quomodo alienus erat Pharisaeis, proprius deus Iudaicae gentis? si ergo haec non cadunt in creatorem, sed in mamonam, 'quis uobis credet quod uerius est'? et 'quis uobis dabit quod meum est'? non potest quasi ali{en)us dixisse de alterius dei gratia. tunc enim uideretur ita dixisse, si eos in creatorem, non in mamonam infideles notando per creatoris mentionem distinctione se fecisset dei alterius, non commissuri suam ueritatem infidelibus creatoris, t quoniam tunc alterius uideri potest, si non ad hoc proponatur, ut a re, de qua agitur, separetur. Si autem et iustificantes se coram hominibus Pharisaei spem mercedis in homine ponebant, illo eos sensu increpabat, quo et propheta Hieremias: miser homo, qui spem habet in homine. si et adicit: scit autem deus corda uestra, illius dei uim commemorabat, (qui) lucernam se pronuntiarat scrutantem renes et corda. si superbiam tangit: quod elatum est apud homines perosum est deo, Esaiam ponit ante oculos: dies enim domini Sabaoth in omnem contumeliosum et superbum, in omnem sublimem et elatum, et humiliabuntur. Possum iam colligere, cur tanto aeuo deus Marcionis fuerit in occulto. expectabat, opinor, donec haec omnia disceret a creatore. didicit igitur usque ad Iohannis tempora atque ita exinde processit adnuntiare regnum dei dicens: lex et prophetae usque ad Iohannem; ex quo regnum dei adnuntiatur. quasi non et nos limitem quendam agnoscamus Iohannem constitutum inter uetera et noua, ad quem desineret Iudaismus et a quo inciperet Christianismus, non tamen, ut ab alia uirtute facta sit sedatio legis et prophetarum et initiatio euangelii, in quo est dei regnum.' [Christus ipse.] nam id si probauimus, et uetera transitura et noua successura praedicari a creatore, si et Iohannes antecursor et praeparator ostenditur uiarum domini euangelium', superducturi et regnum dei promulgaturi, et ex hoc iam, quod Iohannes uenit, ipse erit Christus qui Iohannem erit subsecutus ut antecursorem; et, si desierunt uetera et coeperunt ! noua interstite Iohanne, non erit mirum quod ex dispositione est creatoris, ut unde(unde) magis probetur ** quam ex legis et prophetarum in Iohannem occasu et exinde ortu regni dei. transeat igitur caelum et terra citius, sicut et lex et: prophetae, quam unus apexuerborum domini-nerbum enim, inquit Esaias, dei nostri manet in aeuum —: nam quoniam in Esaia iam tunc Christus, sermo scilicet et spiritus creatoris, Iohannem praedicarat — uocem clamantis in deserto: parate uiam domini — in hoc uenturum, ut legis et] prophetarum ordo exinde cessaret, per adimpletionem, non per destructionem, et regnum dei a Christo adnuntiaretur, I ideo subtexuit facilius elementa transitura quam uerba sua,' confirmans hoc quoque, quod de Iohanne dixerat, non praeterisse.
pass_a_gloss: To whom he denies that it is possible to serve two lords, because it is necessary to offend one and defend the other, he himself declares, proposing God and mammon. Therefore, mammon, which he wants to be understood, if you do not have an interpreter, you can learn from him. For, admonishing us to look out for worldly friendships according to the example of that servant, who, having been removed from office, relieves the lord's debtors by diminishing their securities for his own benefit: and I, he says, tell you, make friends for yourselves from mammon of injustice, namely from money, from which also that servant. For we know that money is the author and ruler of all worldly injustice. Seeing the covetousness of the Pharisees, he strengthened this sentence: you cannot serve God and mammon. Finally, the Pharisees, who were greedy for money, ridiculed, because they understood, of course, that mammon was spoken of in terms of money, lest they think that the creator is to be understood in mammon and that Christ recalled them from the service of the creator. What now? Rather, learn from this that Christ showed one God. For he named two lords, God and mammon, the creator and money: finally, you cannot serve God, certainly to him whom they seemed to serve, and mammon, to whom they were more devoted. But if he himself were acting as another, he would have demonstrated not two lords, but three — and the creator is indeed the lord, because he is God, and certainly a greater lord than mammon, and more to be obeyed by man, because he is a greater lord —; what kind of thing is it, that he who said mammon was lord and joined him with the true Lord, would be silent about the Lord himself, that is, the creator God? Or did he, by being silent, concede that he should be served, if only he denied that it is possible to serve him and mammon? Thus, when he sets forth one God, naming also the creator, if he himself were another, he named the creator, whom he set forth as lord without another God. And therefore, it will become clear how it was said: if you have not been faithful in mammon of injustice, what is true, who will trust you? Certainly in unjust money, not in the creator, whom Marcion also makes just, and: if you have not been found faithful in what is another's, who will give you what is mine? For what is another's must be unjust, and separated from the semi-God. But how was the creator alien to the Pharisees, when he was the proper God of the Jewish people? If, therefore, these things do not fall upon the creator, but upon mammon, who will trust you with what is truer? And who will give you what is mine? He cannot have said this as if it were another's, concerning the grace of another God. For then he would seem to have said this, if he had noted them as unfaithful in the creator, not in mammon, by mentioning the creator, making a distinction between the God of another, not entrusting his truth to the unfaithful of the creator. But if the Pharisees, justifying themselves before men, placed their hope of reward in men, he rebuked them with that sense in which also the prophet Jeremiah: woe to the man who puts his hope in man. And if he adds: but God knows your hearts, he commemorated the power of that God, who declared himself to be the searcher of kidneys and hearts. If he touches on pride: what is exalted among men is an abomination to God, he sets Isaiah before their eyes: for the day of the Lord of hosts will be upon every arrogant and haughty one, and they will be humbled. I can now gather why the God of Marcion was in hiding for so long. He was waiting, I think, until he learned all these things from the creator. Therefore, he learned up to the time of John and thus proceeded to announce the kingdom of God, saying: the law and the prophets were until John; from whom the kingdom of God is announced. As if we do not recognize a certain boundary established by John between the old and the new, at which Judaism ceased and Christianity began, not, however, that the cessation of the law and the prophets and the initiation of the gospel, in which is the kingdom of God, was made by another virtue, but by Christ himself. For if we have proven this, that the old things are passing away and the new things are succeeding, as predicted by the creator, and John is shown to be the forerunner and preparer of the ways of the Lord, and the gospel and the kingdom of God are to be proclaimed, and from this it is already clear that, since John came, Christ himself will be the one who followed John as a forerunner; and if the old things ceased and the new things began with John in between, it will not be surprising that this is from the disposition of the creator, so that it may be proven more than from the passing away of the law and the prophets in John and from the rising of the kingdom of God. Therefore, let heaven and earth pass away more quickly, just as also the law and the prophets, than one dot of the Lord's words — for the word of our God remains forever —; for since in Isaiah Christ, namely the word and spirit of the creator, had already predicted John, saying: a voice crying in the desert: prepare the way of the Lord, he was coming to this, that the order of the law and the prophets would cease from then on, through fulfillment, not destruction, and the kingdom of God would be announced by Christ. Therefore, he more easily undermined the elements that would pass away than his own words, confirming also what he had said about John, that he did not pass away.

choices.why: The Latin word 'mamona' is translated as 'wealth, riches' to convey the idea of material possessions.
The Latin word 'deus' is translated as 'God' to refer to the supreme being.

pass_b_english: He denies that anyone can serve two masters, because you inevitably offend one to defend the other, and he makes his point by naming them: God and Mammon. So if you lack an interpreter for what he means by Mammon, you can learn it from him directly. He warns us to secure our worldly friendships by following the example of that steward who, once fired, reduced his master's debtors' obligations to feather his own nest. 'And I tell you,' he says, 'make friends for yourselves with the mammon of unrighteousness' — that is, with money, the very stuff that steward used (Luke 16:13). We all know money is the author and tyrant of all worldly injustice. When he saw the Pharisees' greed, he drove the point home: 'You cannot serve God and mammon.' The money-loving Pharisees sneered, precisely because they grasped that 'mammon' meant money — lest anyone think the Creator was meant by 'mammon' and that Christ had called them out of the Creator's service.

So learn this instead: Christ revealed one God. He named two lords — God and Mammon, the Creator and money — and said, 'You cannot serve God,' meaning the One they appeared to serve, 'and mammon,' the one they actually served. If Christ were playing for a different team, he would have had to present not two lords but three — since the Creator is Lord by virtue of being God, and a greater Lord than Mammon, more binding on man precisely because he is greater. What sense would it make for the one who called Mammon a lord and paired him with the true Lord to then fall silent about the Lord himself, the Creator God? Or did his silence concede that the Creator should be served, simply because he denied you can serve both him and Mammon? By positing one God and naming the Creator as that God, he shows that if he were someone else, he would have named the Creator as Lord without any other God beside him.

Therefore it becomes clear how the saying works: 'If you have not been faithful in unrighteous mammon, who will entrust you with what is true?' (Luke 16:11). That means unrighteous money, not the Creator — whom Marcion also declares just. 'And if you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?' What belongs to another must be the unjust thing, alien to the demiurge. But how was the Creator 'alien' to the Pharisees when he was the proper God of the Jewish nation? If these charges don't stick to the Creator but to Mammon, then 'who will trust you with what is truer?' and 'who will give you what is mine?' He could not have spoken as if it were another's, concerning the grace of another God. For that would only make sense if he had indicted them for unfaithfulness to the Creator, not to Mammon, and by invoking the Creator drawn a line between himself and another God, withholding his truth from the Creator's unfaithful.

When the Pharisees justified themselves before men and pinned their hope of reward on human approval, he rebuked them with the same sensibility as the prophet Jeremiah: 'Wretched is the man who trusts in man.' When he adds, 'But God knows your hearts,' he invokes the power of that God who declared himself the searcher of kidneys and hearts. When he strikes at pride — 'What is exalted among men is an abomination to God' — he sets Isaiah before their eyes: 'For the day of the Lord of Hosts comes upon every arrogant and haughty one, upon everyone lifted high, and they shall be humbled.'

I can now see why Marcion's God stayed hidden for so long. He was waiting, I suspect, until he had learned all this from the Creator. So he took notes up to John's time, then launched his announcement of the kingdom of God with the line: 'The Law and the Prophets were until John; from then on the kingdom of God is proclaimed.' As if we don't also recognize John as the boundary marker set between old and new, where Judaism stops and Christianity starts — not because a different power brought the Law and Prophets to a close and inaugurated the Gospel where God's kingdom resides, but Christ himself. If we have proved that the old passes and the new succeeds as predicted by the Creator, and John is shown to be the forerunner and preparer of the Lord's ways, to usher in the Gospel and proclaim the kingdom of God, then from John's arrival it follows that Christ is the one who came after John as his forerunner. And if the old ended and the new began with John as the hinge, it should not surprise us that this came from the Creator's own design — so that it might be proved even more decisively than by the Law and Prophets' sunset in John and the kingdom's sunrise from there.

Therefore let heaven and earth pass away sooner than one dot of the Lord's words — 'for the word of our God stands forever' —; since in Isaiah, Christ, the Word and Spirit of the Creator, had already foretold John: 'A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord' (Isaiah 40:3). He was coming to bring the order of the Law and Prophets to an end through fulfillment, not destruction, and to announce the kingdom of God through Christ. That is why he more easily undermined the elements destined to pass away than his own words, confirming also what he had said about John: that John would not pass away.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the distinction between the Creator and Mammon. Scripture citations (Luke 16:13, Luke 16:11, Isaiah 40:3) are correctly identified and applied to the relevant Latin clauses. Pass A preserves the clause structure and sense of the Latin, and Pass B provides a fluent English rendering that adheres to the meaning of Pass A and the source without adding external content or contradicting the text.

source: 'mamonam quem intellegi uelit, si interpretem non habes, ab ipso potes discere.', English: 'Therefore, mammon, which he wants to be understood, if you do not have an interpreter, you can learn from him.'
